entries.title: Prosecutors Say Probe Into Ilhan Omar Goes Back to the 1980s
entries.summary: Newly unsealed court records center on a fight over sensitive legislative records in the raid of Omar’s Washington home.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Monday unsealed some records connected to the Trump administration’s ongoing investigation into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar for alleged immigration fraud, much of it dealing with a fight over constitutional questions about the search of the congresswoman’s Washington home.

While most of the 169 pages unsealed are heavily redacted, at least one shows prosecutors say their investigation looks back to Omar in the 1980s when she was a child.

In seeking a warrant to raid Omar’s Washington home, prosecutors clashed with U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh over protections for the congresswoman’s sensitive legislative records days before agents showed up in the early-morning hours at her house, the newly released records show. Justice Department attorneys then sought to keep Sharbaugh’s criticism sealed.

Neither Omar nor any of her family members have been charged in connection with the investigation, though several of her relatives have received grand jury subpoenas from the Justice Department.

The dispute revealed in the documents centers on the Constitution’s Speech and Debate Clause, which protects Congress from interference by the executive branch. The Justice Department argued that because the investigation concerned Omar’s private life, it did not need to follow special search procedures for her congressional files.

Sharbaugh disagreed. On Oct. 9, he ordered prosecutors to add extra safeguards, giving Omar a chance to identify congressionally related materials before the Oct. 12 raid.

“No matter how small the potential volume of legislative materials at issue, the constitutional protections remain,” Sharbaugh wrote on Oct. 15, adding that prosecutors failed to revise their plans in response to his concerns. “Instead, it stood pat on its existing proposed search protocols without further modification.”

The documents released also included a supplemental brief — prepared by the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro — supporting the request for a warrant to search Omar’s Washington residence.

The brief reveals that the government applied for the warrant on Oct. 2, 10 days before Homeland Security Investigations agents raided Omar’s D.C. home and seized 17 items including cell phones, laptops and passports.

Prosecutors claimed they had “a rock-solid basis to issue the warrant,” describing alleged violations involving Omar "occurring between 1980 and the present.”

Three days after the raid, Sharbaugh moved to release his explanation of the dispute over federal search procedures.

The Justice Department objected, calling his account “an incomplete and flawed summary of what occurred,” according to the unsealed records.

“The United States believes ILHAN has committed (redacted) crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress,” Pirro wrote in her arguments against unsealing the court records.

More than half of pages in the release are completely or heavily redacted, including several pages with the label “Special Search Procedures” — the revised procedures Sharbaugh ordered the DOJ to prepare. The 67-page affidavit laying out the government’s evidence also remains sealed.

The entire case has been under seal since federal authorities raided Omar’s D.C. home last month, but a coalition of news organizations, including The Washington Sun, filed to unseal the records. The Justice Department has argued against releasing them, telling the federal court it could jeopardize the criminal investigation into Omar.

“How a search warrant was executed—including what was seized and anything Ms. Omar said or admitted during the search—are precisely the sort of highly sensitive facts that shouldn’t be made public during an ongoing investigation that has yet to yield a charging decision,” Pirro argued.

James Boasberg, the chief judge of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, considered the news organizations’ applications in a hearing Tuesday. While he agreed that a “vast majority” of the search warrant should remain sealed, Boasberg questioned why information about any efforts to safeguard Omar’s constitutional rights through the course of the investigation should be kept confidential.

During the hearing, Boasberg ordered the Justice Department to submit a redaction proposal by Friday for the court to consider before releasing the documents Monday. The judge also appeared skeptical of the DOJ’s argument that its search warrant records should not be released because it had not been fully completed — even though the warrant had been returned to the magistrate judge, a common practice when executing such orders.

After the raid, the Minnesota congresswoman immediately characterized the operation as an “outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies” in a post on X.

Omar was born in Somalia, but she and her family fled the country after a civil war began there in 1991. She became a U.S. citizen in 2000. The HSI raid was part of a probe into potential immigration fraud and questions about citizenship paperwork Omar’s late father prepared in 1995.

President Donald Trump’s top immigration officials have continued to speak publicly about the substantial evidence the government allegedly has to support the investigation into Omar. White House border czar Tom Homan said after the raid that he had been told that HSI has “a strong case,” while Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin described the evidence against Omar as “strong.”

Trump has said he had “nothing to do” with the investigation, but he has repeatedly called for Omar to resign from Congress — alleging she used a “fake” name when she was sworn in. A spokesperson from Omar’s office pushed back against the statements last month, calling them “flat out false.”

This story has been updated with further information from the unsealed documents.

entries.title: The Commanders Make a Little Magic in a 22-20 Win Over the Bengals
entries.summary: A frenzied final drive led to a game-winning field goal as Washington upset red-hot Cincinnati.
entries.content:
There has been near-constant chatter this season about the Commanders' need for receiver help. It started in the offseason and only grew louder when veteran Terry McLaurin went down with an injury in Week 6.

As it turns out, Washington may have had the solution on its roster this whole time.

Late on Monday night, rookie Antonio Williams hauled in a 42-yard pass with the clock ticking down, capping a sterling 122-yard performance and giving his team a short field goal attempt to win a game that had seemed lost just seconds before. Drew Stevens nailed that 26-yarder and the Commanders beat the seemingly unbeatable Bengals, 22-20.

"I personally live for those moments — high pressure situations," quarterback Jayden Daniels said. "You want to go out there and make your mark on the game."

https://x.com/NFL/status/2125081616204599547
The win was made possible on defense, where Washington limited the league's hottest offense to a modest output. Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, the Bengals' star wideouts, combined for just 74 yards.

Up front, defensive coordinator Daronte Jones decided he would blitz, blitz again and blitz some more. The Commanders hit Joe Burrow 10 times and sacked him three times, keeping pressure on the MVP candidate and forcing him into quick, short throws. Outside of a 31-yard touchdown to Higgins in the second quarter, the defensive backs — led by replacement starter Rasul Douglas — limited game-changing plays.

The Commanders' offense took a little while to get going. High snaps, blown assignments and an inability to stop Cincinnati linebacker Boye Mafe (three sacks) hampered the unit throughout the first half. Washington went into the break with just one third-down conversion. At one point, receiver Stefon Diggs was seen on the broadcast yelling in frustration on the sideline.

But maybe there’s a method to Diggs’ madness, because after gaining just 28 net yards through the first 28 minutes of the game, the Commanders' offense went on a nine-play, 79-yard drive at the end of the first half to get on the board and cut the score to 10-7.

The momentum of that drive carried over into the first few minutes of the second half, when Daniels broke off a 47-yard scramble to set up a game-tying field goal.

But Washington was never able to pull away, and Cincinnati took a 20-19 lead on a 56-yard field goal from Evan McPherson with 46 seconds left. Washington got the ball back with no timeouts remaining and little reason to believe in its comeback chances.

Williams started the frenzied final drive with a 21-yard grab. After a spike, Daniels (289 yards passing and 55 yards rushing) targeted the rookie out of Clemson again, hitting him over the middle of the field. Williams sprinted down into the red zone, setting up Stevens' short, game-winning kick.

https://x.com/NFL/status/2125081931981209908
"To see those guys come through at the end, I thought that was one of our best team wins," coach Dan Quinn said.

The Commanders (4-5-1) scored their first consecutive wins since the 2024 playoffs, and things are now looking up: Their next two opponents, the Cardinals and Titans, have just four wins between them.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Housing on Hold
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 24, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Chevy Chase Library, Metro snooping and a big win for the Commanders.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 5/10. Quite a comedown from Monday’s 70-degree weather. Sunshine helps save the day, but breezes have bite. Read the full forecast.




THE LATEST

Could new housing be (Chevy) chased out of one of D.C.’s wealthiest areas?

Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George is putting a hold on outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser’s plan to build new housing atop a modernized library and recreation center in Chevy Chase, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports.

Her decision throws the proposal's fate into doubt. The project had prompted fierce debate in the tony Ward 3 neighborhood, which has generally lagged behind other parts of the city in building both market-rate and affordable housing.

“I want to see new proposals, new opportunities presented that embody the community’s needs,” Lewis George told The Sun, referring to the Chevy Chase project and a proposed redevelopment plan of the old Fletcher-Johnson school in Ward 7, which she is also shelving.

Bowser initially floated the idea of putting housing on top of a new library and rec center five years ago, saying it would give more people the chance to live in the neighborhood while also addressing historic exclusionary housing policies that kept many Black residents out.

But opponents have said the resulting building would be too big and the library and rec center too small and called Bowser’s proposal a sweetheart giveaway of public land to a private developer.

“I think it's a shame,” said Ward 3 council member Matt Frumin. “People talk about the need to build housing, and this is an opportunity to build housing and an opportunity to deliver a great rec center and library.”

Lewis George hasn’t said whether she wants to tweak Bowser’s plans for 177 units of housing or completely revamp them. But any significant delay in the Chevy Chase project could also work against the mayor-elect’s pledge to build 72,000 new housing units across D.C. to help bring down the cost of housing. She has also promoted building more housing in wealthy neighborhoods that have often fought development.

Chevy Chase Library 1 (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)




DEEP DIVE

D.C. government veteran Karim Marshall is running for the Ward 4 council seat Lewis George will vacate in January, The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports. Marshall, 46, said he’s running as a Democrat this time. He is the director of climate and energy policy at the Consumer Federation of America and previously served as a Biden-era environmental justice adviser at the EPA. In 2022, he placed fifth in the at-large race as an independent.

Marshall said he is campaigning at the ward level this cycle to be more hands-on with constituents, flagging energy costs and the city’s next budget and comprehensive plan as early priorities. With no special election date set, the Manor Park resident said he plans to declare today and kick off a “listening tour” throughout the ward.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A pilot program meant to help tenants and landlords avoid D.C.’s protracted eviction process by going through mediation and receiving rental assistance barely squeaked through its human services committee markup yesterday. It faces uncertain prospects before the full council, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports. Council members Zachary Parker, Christina Henderson and Wendell Felder expressed doubts that the pilot would be more than a band-aid to the District’s profound rental nonpayment crisis, and all pledged to vote it down unless changes were made.

Frumin, the chair of the committee, maintained that the pilot is not intended as a solution to the housing crisis but would provide some much-needed relief to backlogged District courts. “We made absolutely sure that this didn’t slow an eviction process, it created an opening for the landlord and the tenant to come together and to try to come to a solution,” Frumin said.

Sneak peek: A Metro rider spotted comprehensive plans to overhaul the Smithsonian National Museum of American History on a Trump staffer’s laptop while traveling on the Orange Line, ProPublica reports. The plans included firing director Anthea Hartig, building a statue of George Washington at the museum’s entrance and introducing new exhibits lauding “Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and “Great Families of American History.”

Check, please: D.C.’s auditor found that more than half of the District’s restaurants did not receive a routine health inspection in fiscal year 2025, Washingtonian reports.

A federal judge extended the temporary restraining order that blocks the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Park through Dec. 12, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. Judge Ana Reyes ordered the extension on Monday before the initial restraining order expired on Nov. 28. Reyes also scheduled a Dec. 8 hearing to argue over a preliminary injunction that would further prevent the golf course’s closure. 





FROM VIRGINIA

The Fairfax County Police Department arrested an ATF civilian employee for allegedly impersonating a police officer, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports. An officer said he observed a Dodge Ram pickup truck with emergency lights pull over a vehicle, speak with the driver, then turn off the flashing lights and drive away.





FROM MARYLAND

“Recipe for disaster”: An analysis of ICE operations in Maryland by The Baltimore Banner — which included reviewing more than 500 habeas corpus petitions filed in federal court — found that the agency has been repeatedly accused of using unmarked vehicles to chase and surround people, even if they hadn’t committed any traffic violations.





PENTHOUSES YOU CAN GET FOR UNDER $750,000

DMV real estate MD (2048x1365, AR: 1.50)
This week’s real estate column looks at D.C.-area penthouses listed for less than $750,000.




Where is this house listed? Click on your guess to see the answer:

A. Maryland

B. Virginia

C. D.C.





SPORTS

Commanders 22, Bengals 20. Washington scored an improbable and impressive win on “Monday Night Football.” Down by one point with less than a minute remaining, Jayden Daniels found rookie Antonio Williams (nine catches for 122 yards) on two big pass plays to set up a game-winning field goal by kicker Drew Stevens. The Commanders, winners of two straight for the first time since the 2024 playoffs, move to 4-5-1. The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson takes a closer look at how Washington pulled off its biggest win of the season.

Not wasting any time, the Spirit fired coach Adrián González on Monday — just two days after playing for a NWSL championship, The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports. After a 2-1 loss to the Kansas City Current — the franchise’s third straight finals defeat — the team’s president of soccer operations said “all parties believe a change in leadership is necessary to build on that success and achieve our long-term sporting goals.”

What to Watch Today

NCAAM: Maryland vs. Tennessee, 3 p.m. (ESPN)

NCAAW: Maryland vs. Monmouth, 7 p.m. (B1G+)

NBA: Wizards vs. Celtics, 8 p.m. (Peacock)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: Antonio Williams Has Become ‘Clutch’ For Washington, and Just in Time
entries.summary: The rookie wide receiver has emerged as a favorite target of Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels.
entries.content:
For a few breathless moments, it felt like 2024 again.

With less than a minute to go at Northwest Stadium, Jayden Daniels calmly climbed the pocket and stepped into the role he loves most: the hero. He found his go-to target once, then located him again seconds later in a pivotal march down the field.

That target, wide receiver Antonio Williams, had the most memorable game of his young career in Washington’s 22-20 win over Cincinnati Monday night. Amid a season characterized by missed opportunities and late-game collapses, the 22-year-old rookie provided the excitement that Commanders fans have been craving since the team’s NFC Championship run two seasons ago.

In the span of 39 seconds, with no timeouts to their name, Daniels connected with Williams twice to set up Drew Stevens’ game-winning field goal to stun Joe Burrow and the Bengals in primetime for the second time in three years. The closing drive culminated a nine-catch, 122-yard game for Williams.

“[Williams] is like a little brother to me, so super proud of him,” Daniels said at the podium after the win. “I think the first 100-yard game of his career, so many more for him, but super proud for Tone, man.”

For the first time since that unforgettable 2024 campaign, Daniels and company picked up consecutive victories. Their season, on the brink of despair after Cincinnati took a late lead with less than a minute to play, was given new life. The Commanders now sit two games behind the Giants in the NFC East and hold the tiebreaker against their division rivals following last Thursday’s 24-21 win. And in Williams, a third-round pick in this year’s draft, the Commanders might have found a fix for the issues they’ve had at the receiver position since Terry McLaurin was lost for the year.

“When your number is called, you just gotta execute,” Williams told reporters after the victory. “Trust is earned, so I am just trying to earn that trust from Jayden and the coaching staff.”

On the first play, Daniels zipped a pass to a streaking Williams over the middle of the field for a 22-yard gain. After clocking the ball with 24 seconds left, he found Williams again for 42 more yards — and the rookie dropped to the turf just in time for Daniels to stop the clock with one more spike.

“I thought this was his best performance,” head coach Dan Quinn said of Williams. “I thought he was just clutch tonight, and made some big plays in some big moments. He’s demonstrated that in a lot of instances, so it was good to see him deliver tonight.”

Washington’s offense was by no means a well-oiled machine for much of the rainy late-night slugfest. The Commanders looked frustrated at times — veteran receiver Stefon Diggs made halftime headlines with a passionate moment on the sideline in the second quarter — and Daniels totaled just 74 net passing yards in the first half.

“[The Bengals] had a really good plan,” Daniels said. “We had some answers for their cover zero, they checked out a couple stuff, but they had a really good plan. … A very good team over there, so shoutout to them.”

But the Commanders never folded in the second half. They struggled to make plays in the red zone — all of Washington’s second-half points came from the foot of Stevens, who nailed five field goals.

His fourth boot gave the Commanders a two-point lead with less than three minutes to play, but it also gave Burrow the ball with the chance to potentially ice the game.

“It was back-and-forth to go, but I just thought this was the right time to take a lead,” Quinn said. “We were still above the two-minute, I think had we not been I probably would’ve gone the other way. … I didn’t want to have the game end where we didn’t have another shot at it.”

The Bengals kicked a field goal to take the lead, and Daniels got his shot. The third-year quarterback, who after the game said that he “lives” for the big moments, put his faith in Williams with the game on the line. The rookie rewarded his trust.

“The kid got open,” Daniels said. “He got open, so that’s my job — to find an open person.”

entries.title: Democrat Victoria Broderick Unseats Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee
entries.summary: The Republican has been in the U.S. House since 2010.
entries.content:
Democrat Victoria Broderick defeated eight-term Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais in Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District by a margin of less than 400 votes, AP projected on Tuesday.

Broderick’s victory gives Democrats 259 seats in the U.S. House — a record-breaking majority the party has not seen since last century. The Tennessee Democrat’s win also marks the 47th House seat flip for Democrats this cycle.

entries.title: A Fight Over Hemp Is Complicating the Senate’s Spending Plan
entries.summary: The White House has asked for language to preserve the availability of “non-intoxicating full-spectrum CBD products.”
entries.content:
The White House and a group of Senate Republicans are clashing over a deadline for the future of the hemp-derived products industry, which could have many of its products banned on Dec. 11 unless Congress acts.

The White House put the topic on a list of issues it wants Congress to include in a stopgap spending bill, saying it wants to find language that would preserve the availability of “non-intoxicating full-spectrum CBD products.”

Language would include “guardrails to prevent against such products reaching children while preserving the Congress’s intent to restrict the sale of products that pose serious health risks,” according to a list of administration requests obtained by The Washington Sun.

But a group of Republicans are opposing it, saying it could complicate passage of the spending bill to keep the government open past Dec. 11. “If the administration pushes for yet another delay of the ban—which it promised not to do in August—this misplaced priority will threaten the entire bill,” Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) said on X.

Cotton is among 14 Republicans who sent a letter Monday to the White House that said the law that closes the so-called hemp “loophole” should be allowed to go into effect.

“The choice is simple: stand with American families who don’t want candy-flavored drugs sold in gas stations or with the cartel who profits from addiction and devastation,” the letter says. “There can be no last-minute ‘framework’ that keeps these drugs on store shelves.”

The issue started in the 2018 farm bill, where Congress made hemp legal so farmers could grow it for rope, clothing and food. Upon passage, the rule allowed for any product containing up to 0.3% of delta-9 THC, the main intoxicating ingredient, to be classified as hemp and not marijuana.

This left an opening where items could be sold with less than 0.3% of delta-9 but include other compounds with similar or greater intoxicating properties. Quickly after the law passed, drinks, gummies and vapes with intoxicating properties began selling at convenience stores even in states where marijuana remained illegal.

Last year, Congress changed the rule in a way that has threatened the future of the hemp industry more broadly, counting all forms of THC together, not just delta-9, and capping the amount allowed at 0.4 milligrams per container — an incredibly small amount. This would effectively ban not just drinks and gummies but also creams, oils and balms with trace amounts of THC that are not ingested.

In June, the Office of Management and Budget asked Congress to ensure "fair treatment of hemp products" by revising the provision or, at minimum, extending implementation past Nov. 12, with Congress obliging with a delay until Dec. 11 in September.

Industry trade groups estimate that 95% of the hemp-based cannabinoid industry would be impacted by the rule change. The groups say they welcome additional regulation that sets clear rules and testing requirements but doesn’t take aim at the hemp industry generally with one stroke.

“Opponents are using the real problem of unregulated, synthetic ‘gas station weed’ to argue for treating the entire hemp category the same way,” Farm Aid Inc. and a group of hemp farmers said in a letter to Congress on Monday. “But the bad actors driving that concern, largely synthetic and chemically converted cannabinoids sold with no testing, no labeling, and no age controls, operate outside the responsible, tested, and compliant products our members produce and sell.”.

American Farmers harvested $739 million worth of hemp in 2025, according to the Department of Agriculture.
